input.text: For what it's worth, although this problem might be a bit misplaced, I think it is very nice.  While looking through the test a few days ago, I was fully prepared to crank out a huge coordinate bash (and question whether this was supposed to be on the AMC12 instead) until I saw the symmetry.  Reminds me of #17 from the 2015 AMC 10A, in the sense that the setup of coordinates in the problem statement hides a purely geometric solution in reality.

input.text:
I solved it during the competition, as did one other  on my team

The solution sketch is as follows:

For each point there is a line going through it that cuts the remaining points into two groups that differ in size at most 1.

Take such a line. I claim it works.

Let P be a point. There is such a line l through it. At some point, the windmill will be parallel to that line (COUNTING ORIENTATION.) At this point, it must be l, or else not both of them can split them in such a way (Remember, everything requires orientation.)

In my opinion is very nice problem.

Alternatively if you didn't see the slick solution at first you can just add up the cubes on two of the sides, minus the column of cubes that they both share, then add on the remaining $10^2=100$ cubes on the other side to get:

$2\cdot{11^2}-11+100=11(2\cdot{11}-1)+100=11\cdot{21}+100=231+100=\boxed{331}\rightarrow{\boxed{\mathbf{D}}}$.
